idiom_name: degenerate visitor base + one visitor interface per element + runtime type test in accept
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: make the visitor base an empty marker type (giving it one virtual member in languages that need a polymorphic type), declare one visitor interface per concrete element with a single visit operation on it, let every element expose accept(Visitor) that tests at runtime whether the visitor satisfies the element's own visitor interface, and let concrete visitors declare only the interfaces they actually implement. The test replaces the classic visitor's required method set: a visitor that does not implement the element's interface is simply not called, so partial visitation is normal and no element ever depends on the visitor implementation. The pattern pays off exactly when the element hierarchy is volatile and recompilation costs are real. In C++, use dynamic_cast for the cross-cast; in languages without RTTI, use a type-index dictionary (std::unordered_map<std::type_index, void*>) as a slower but RTTI-free alternative. Prefer pointer-based casts (dynamic_cast<X*>(&v)) over reference-based casts (dynamic_cast<X&>(v)) — a null pointer from a failed cast is a clean null check, while a failed reference cast throws std::bad_cast and forces exception handling into every accept path.
code_sketch:
abstract type Visitor                     # degenerate: no visit methods at all
interface CircleVisitor: Visitor { visit(Circle) }   # one per element
class Circle: Shape:
    accept(visitor: Visitor):
        if visitor is CircleVisitor cv: cv.visit(self)   # failed test == not handled
class AreaVisitor: CircleVisitor, RectVisitor:           # only what it handles
    visit(Circle): ...
    visit(Rect): ...
pitfalls: Letting an element name a concrete visitor, or a visitor name a concrete element it does not handle, reintroduces the dependency cycle the pattern exists to break.
Silence on the failed test is the default in every language; log, count or assert on the unhandled element/visitor pair so missing coverage is observable.
The degenerate base must stay empty; a default or catch-all visit method on it turns the pattern back into a classic visitor and hides which elements a visitor really supports.

In C++, prefer dynamic_cast<X*>(&v) over dynamic_cast<X&>(v): a null pointer is a clean null check, while a failed reference cast throws std::bad_cast and pollutes every accept path with exception-handling overhead.

The cross-cast (dynamic_cast across an inheritance hierarchy, not down the same tree) is the only form that works here; a downcast to a derived type that is not actually in the visitor's inheritance graph is undefined behaviour in some implementations.
When element counts grow large, hand-written accept methods become a maintenance burden; use a code generator or macro to emit them uniformly rather than duplicating the same three-line pattern.
The degenerate base's single virtual destructor is not cosmetic — it is the gateway to RTTI; omitting it or making it non-virtual breaks dynamic_cast in C++.

Partial visitation means a visitor that should handle a new element but was written before that element existed will silently skip it; cover this with integration tests that traverse representative object graphs with all element types present.
